what: A vector index finds the stored embeddings closest to a query embedding without comparing against every one. It trades a little accuracy (recall) for huge speed, using structures like HNSW graphs or IVF clusters.
like: Like finding a friend's house by asking neighbours who live nearer and nearer, instead of knocking on every door in the city.
why: Semantic search: finds passages that mean the same thing, even with different words
Answers in milliseconds over millions or billions of vectors (approximate nearest neighbour, ANN)
The first stage of RAG: a cheap wide net before an expensive reranker and the LLM

nodes.t: HNSW graph|layers, M links per node
Full vectors|float32 on disk or S3

steps.d: The same embedding model used for the documents turns the query into a vector. Mixing models breaks everything, because the two vector spaces do not line up.
HNSW starts at a sparse top layer, hops greedily to closer neighbours, then drops a layer and repeats. ef_search sets how many candidates it keeps while walking.
Distances during the walk use compressed vectors: int8, or 1-bit as in Elastic BBQ (32x smaller). They fit in RAM and are fast, but slightly blurry.
Post-filtering after the walk can leave fewer than k results. Better engines filter during the walk (ACORN) or keep scanning until enough matches appear.
Oversample, for example 3x: ask for 30 candidates when k is 10, then re-rank them with the full float vectors. This wins back most of the lost recall.
New vectors go to a write log, become searchable segments and are merged in the background. Deletes are marked first and cleaned up during merges.

numbers.l: pgvector HNSW defaults: m, ef_construction, ef_search
smaller vectors with Elastic BBQ: float32 down to 1 bit
default BBQ oversample: k=10 fetches 30 to rescore
vectors allowed in one Amazon S3 Vectors index
turbopuffer warm query p50 at 1M docs; cold ~874 ms

choices.d: More links per node (M) and a wider build list give a better graph and higher recall, at the cost of slower builds and more memory.
The main query-time knob. Raise it and recall@10 climbs while latency rises. Tune it against a labelled eval set, not by feel.
float32 is exact but large. int8 is a safe default. 1-bit (BBQ, RaBitQ-style) saves the most memory but needs oversample plus rescore.
Pre-filter (search only allowed ids), post-filter (search then drop), or filter during the walk. Very selective filters need the last one or a separate index per tenant.
All in RAM (fastest, priciest), on SSD (DiskANN, DiskBBQ), or on object storage with a cache (S3 Vectors, turbopuffer) for big, cold, cheap data.

instead.why: Exact words, names and codes: BM25 beats embeddings there
Run BM25 and vectors together and fuse the lists (RRF)
Not a replacement: rescores the top 50 to 100 far more precisely
The full database product around the index: storage, replicas, APIs

breaks.d: The graph finds 40 neighbours, the filter drops 38, and only 2 results come back.
breaks.see: Result count below k for selective tenants or filters
breaks.fix: Filter during the walk (ACORN), pgvector iterative scans, or a partition per tenant

breaks.d: Compressed distances reorder close neighbours, so true matches fall out of the top k.
breaks.see: recall@10 on the eval set drops after a mapping change
breaks.fix: Oversample and rescore with full vectors; raise ef_search

breaks.d: HNSW wants its graph and vectors in RAM; once it spills, latency jumps.
breaks.see: p99 latency rising with page faults or disk reads
breaks.fix: Quantise, use a disk-based index, or shard across nodes

breaks.d: Updates and deletes are marked but the graph is rebuilt lazily.
breaks.see: Deleted docs still appearing; recall drifting down over weeks
breaks.fix: Regular merges or reindex; filter deleted ids at query time

breaks.d: New query vectors no longer match old document vectors.
breaks.see: Relevance falls sharply right after a model change
breaks.fix: Re-embed into a new index, dual-write, switch with an alias

say: I'll embed chunks and put them in an HNSW index with int8 or binary quantisation, so the graph fits in RAM.
Retrieval is two stage: oversample about 3x from the ANN index, rescore with full vectors, then a cross-encoder reranks the top 50.
I'll tune ef_search on a labelled set, tracking recall@10 against p99 latency, and pick the cheapest point that meets the target.
For per-tenant filters I'd filter during the graph walk or give big tenants their own partition, so filtered queries still return k results.

followups.a: HNSW gives great recall and latency but costs memory and slow builds. IVF clusters vectors and searches only the nearest lists (probes): cheaper to build and smaller, but recall depends on good clusters and enough probes.

The graph assumes every node is reachable. Removing most nodes breaks the paths, so the walk gets stuck or wanders. Engines fix this by filtering during the walk with extra hops, or falling back to exact search for tiny allowed sets.

followups.q: What does late interaction (ColBERT) cost to store?
followups.a: It keeps one vector per token instead of one per chunk, so storage grows with document length. Teams compress those token vectors hard, or keep them only for reranking a shortlist found by a single-vector index.

followups.q: When would you use S3 Vectors or turbopuffer?
followups.a: Large, mostly cold, many-tenant data where cost matters more than first-query latency. Data lives on object storage and hot namespaces get cached on SSD, so warm queries are fast and storage is cheap.

today: Elasticsearch 9.1 made BBQ the default quantisation for dense vectors of 384 dimensions or more, and added ACORN for filtered vector search, with typical speedups of about 5x.

check.q: You raise ef_search from 40 to 200. What do you expect?
check.why: ef_search is the candidate list kept during the walk: bigger list, more checked, better recall, more time.

check.q: With 1-bit quantisation, how do you win recall back?
check.a: Oversample, then rescore with full vectors
check.why: The cheap pass finds a wider shortlist; exact float distances then pick the true top k.

check.q: A tenant filter leaves only 3 results when you asked for 10. What happened?
check.a: The filter ran after the ANN search
check.why: Post-filtering throws away neighbours found by the walk, so fewer than k survive.

check.q: Which metric shows if your ANN index misses true neighbours?
check.why: Recall compares ANN results to brute-force results on the same queries.
